mcqs.question: A problem asks how many distinct 3-digit PIN prefixes can be formed by picking 3 distinct digits from 0-9 and arranging them in a specific order. Is this a permutation or combination count?
options: A permutation, since two different orderings of the same 3 digits count as different PINs
A combination, since only the set of chosen digits matters
Neither — this requires a separate stars-and-bars calculation
A combination, because digits are being selected from a fixed pool of 10
mcqs.explanation: PIN order matters — 123 and 321 are different PINs from the same 3 digits — so each distinct ordering is a distinct outcome, which is the defining trait of a permutation (nPr), not a combination. "Selected from a fixed pool" alone doesn't determine which one applies; whether order matters does.

mcqs.question: You need to answer 10^5 different nCr(n, r) mod p queries, with n up to 10^6 and p a large prime. Why precompute factorial and inverse-factorial arrays up front instead of computing each query's factorials fresh?
options: Because factorials must be computed in a fixed order to remain valid mod p
Because it caps the per-query cost at O(1) after an O(n) one-time setup, instead of paying O(n) per query for 10^5 queries
Because inverse factorials can only be computed once per program, not once per query
Because Fermat's little theorem only produces a correct answer the first time it's called
mcqs.explanation: Precomputing turns 10^5 queries at O(n) each — potentially 10^11 total operations — into one O(n) setup plus O(1) per query. The other options misstate real constraints: factorial order doesn't need fixing beyond the natural i=1..n build, inverse factorials can be recomputed anytime, and Fermat's theorem is correct on every call, not just the first.

mcqs.question: You need nCr(n, r) mod 12, where 12 is not prime, for a handful of small queries with n under 50. Which approach is safe to use without modification?
options: Factorial plus Fermat's little theorem, since Fermat's theorem works for any modulus
Factorial plus extended-Euclid-based inverse, applied without checking gcd(factorial, 12)
Pascal's triangle table, since it only ever adds two values mod p and never needs an inverse
Neither approach works when the modulus is composite
mcqs.explanation: Pascal's recurrence only adds two already-reduced values mod p, so it never needs a modular inverse or any coprimality condition — it works under any modulus, prime or not. Fermat's theorem explicitly requires a prime modulus, and factorials mod 12 can share factors with 12, so an inverse via extended Euclid isn't guaranteed to exist without checking gcd first.

mcqs.question: A developer computes nCr mod p as (fact[n] // (fact[r] * fact[n-r])) % p, where fact[] values are already stored reduced mod p. What's wrong with this?
options: Nothing — integer division is equivalent to multiplying by a modular inverse here
fact[n-r] should be added to fact[r] instead of multiplied
The formula should use fact[n-1] instead of fact[n]
fact[n], fact[r], and fact[n-r] are residues, not true factorials, so integer-dividing them has no mathematical relationship to the intended division
mcqs.explanation: Once a value is reduced mod p it's a residue, not the original integer, so ordinary integer division on it doesn't recover anything meaningful about the true factorial ratio. The only correct way to "divide" under a modulus is to multiply by the modular inverse of the divisor; the other listed formula changes are unrelated to the actual bug.

mcqs.question: In a 4-column, 3-row grid, you count paths from top-left to bottom-right moving only right or down. Why is the answer nCr(5, 2) rather than nCr(5, 3)?
options: Because only right-moves are countable in this formula, and there are 3 of them, making nCr(5, 3) invalid
Because nCr(5, 3) would double-count paths that revisit a cell
Because the grid's row count determines r directly, regardless of move counts
Because the grid has 5 total moves and you're choosing the 2 down-moves' positions among them (equivalently nCr(5, 3) for the right-moves — both give the same value)
mcqs.explanation: The path has 5 total move-slots (3 right, 2 down); choosing which 2 slots are "down" determines the whole path, and choosing which 3 are "right" describes exactly the same split from the other side — nCr(5,2) and nCr(5,3) are numerically identical (both equal 10) because nCr(n,r) = nCr(n,n-r). Paths never revisit cells by construction, so that isn't a factor.
